title: Become a Better Listener and Gain Clarity With Say More
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece introduces a simple, low-effort alternative to the harder practice of formulating clarifying questions while actively listening: simply asking others to 'say more.' It argues that generating clarifying questions on the fly interrupts a leader's own processing of what's being said, making it a difficult habit to sustain. Prompting someone to elaborate, by contrast, slows the conversation without taxing the listener's thinking, and often yields a more succinct restatement of their point. The article closes with a memorable formulation: the best leaders learn to listen by listening to learn.
points: Active listening requires leaders to slow down and withhold their own views before responding.
Formulating clarifying questions while listening is difficult because it competes with processing what's being said.
Asking others to 'say more' is offered as an easier, equally effective alternative.
Prompting elaboration often produces a more succinct, clearer restatement of the speaker's point.
The technique can become a low-effort conversational habit rather than requiring quick thinking.
quotes: Active listening requires leaders to slow down and process what they hear before responding.
Having to think of a clarifying question while listening interrupts a leader’s processing and sense-making of what is being said.
Examine great listeners, those who make others truly feel heard, and you will find a simple and effective behavior that is present in almost every exchange.
Interestingly, asking others to elaborate further on what they have already said will often result in a more succinct restatement of their comments.
As several authors like to say, the best leaders learn to listen by listening to learn.
